emptyFalls.text: Your foot finds the one soft place on the hill. You get free, and the bog keeps a little of what you carried. You've got one more fall in you, maybe.
A wave you never saw slaps you off the ledge into the swirl, and something rolls out of your bag and is gone. You've got one more ducking in you, maybe.

rescuedLoot.text: The fog comes down and the day goes with it. At dusk a dog finds you first, and then a shepherd with a lantern, who looks at you the way he'd look at a ewe that got itself stuck.
rescuedLoot.say: He walks you down to the road and won't take a penny. "Past the third cairn," he says, shaking his head. "They always go past the third cairn."

rescuedLoot.text: The tide comes in faster than you can go out. You spend hours on a ledge with the sea at your chest, until it turns and lets you crawl for the mouth, and a lighterman out after driftwood hauls you into his boat with a boathook.
rescuedLoot.say: He rows you to the harbour steps and won't take a coin. "On the flood," he says, shaking his head. "They always go in on the ebb and think it'll last."

endingLoot.text: You lead them down off the moor in the late light: Ottilie in her sun hat, asking where her ferns are; a young man in a coat seven years out of date, asking what year it is; and the rest, in shirtsleeves, the scarecrows having their coats, back further than the hedges, quiet and amazed. Behind you, the hill's door is only turf.

The lent walk down off the moor with you at dusk, Ottilie among them complaining about her ferns, and the villages come out to see. You tell the green what you promised the Tenant on their behalf. There's a long silence. Then the miller, of all people, starts to laugh, and fetches his fiddle.

The man in good boots is waiting at the old hall's gate at dusk, as if he'd known. He doesn't ask; he only looks at your face, and smiles, and holds out a purse. "My principals are grateful," he says.  "The upland will do very well now." Behind him, on the moor, the fog sits on the hollow hill like a hand.

warmAfterBreaking: The turf of the hollow hill is warm, the way a loaf is warm under its cloth, though the fog is cold all round it. When you kneel, you can feel something through your knees, very faint and very regular, like a great slow breath.
coldAfterBreaking: Round the far side of the hollow hill, where the door was, there's only turf, and in the grass an iron knocker shaped like a sheaf, rusted through as if it had lain there a hundred years. The hill is cold under your hand. Somewhere a lark goes up, an ordinary bird on an ordinary moor.

daytime.text: The scarecrows stand in their row along the far field, in their very decent coats: good wool, brass buttons, a travelling cloak. Somebody's coats, once. In the dusk you see that every collar has a little name-tape stitched inside, the kind a careful mother sews in.

The man in good boots is drinking with his clerk at the end of the Drovers' Inn's long table, his leather folder at his elbow. He looks up and smiles at you, a practised smile. "Sit. I've bought the old hall, and I'm buying the upland. A word to the wise: the valley's luck is about to change hands. Tell me who the inn's guest is this year, and when they go up the hill, and you'll find me generous."
daytime.say: You tell him about Ottilie, and room seven. He writes it in his folder and pays in gold, more than the words were worth. "The old hall," he says, "if you've more." You walk out into the night with the gold heavy and something else heavier.

daytime.text: Room seven's door is open, and the room is made up fresh: clean sheets, an empty grate, no fern book, no sun hat. You ask the landlord where Miss Venn has gone. "Who?" he says, kindly, puzzled, wiping a glass. "We've no lady of that name. Never had." On the clean floor, under the bed, there's a pressed fern.
daytime.say: "She was here," you say, loud enough for the whole taproom. Nobody looks up. The landlord only smiles, sorry for you, and the room goes on with its evening as if you'd said nothing at all. You walk out with the fern in your fist, glad you said it, and with every eye in the valley on your back.

daytime.text: The hedge-witch is on her steps with the rue in her lap, and for once she meets your eye. "So," she says. "They've taken the fern girl. Sit down." Then she tells you: the Tenant, under the hollow hill on the moor, and the guest it's lent every seventh year. "They'll tell you the lent come home. They don't. They sit at its supper, not a day older, as long as the bargain holds." And the harvests, good, good, good.

firstMillClue: The wheel's turning on the dry race again, and the miller's on his chair beside it with a lantern and a little book, making a mark at every turn, as patient as a man counting sheep. The book looks just like the landlord's.
eveningFernHunt: You spend the afternoon up to your knees in the fen with Ottilie, and she knows the name of everything green and laughs at everything else. You come back soaked to the thigh and fond of her. At the inn door the landlord is waiting with towels, as if he knew when you'd be back.
singleClueBargain: You name its guests, from the book and the collars, and offer better: the whole valley every seventh year, keepers, children and fiddlers, one night, home by morning. The Tenant listens to the end, and laughs, a sound like a full barn. "Done," it says. "Bring the fiddlers."

coatOpenings: The scarecrows in the far field are wearing better coats than you are. Good wool, brass buttons, a travelling cloak with a stitched hem. Somebody's coats, once.
The scarecrows again. One of them has a label inside its collar, from a tailor in the capital.
excludedCoatFinding.coatCallback: The scarecrows stand in their row along the far field, in their very decent coats: good wool, brass buttons, a travelling cloak. Somebody's coats, once. You found a tailor's label in one collar before. In the dusk you see that every collar has a name in it, a little name-tape, the kind a careful mother sews in.
